# Drive Success With Metropolitan.

A Trusted Leader in Final-Mile Delivery

## Premium Furniture Logistics. Nationwide Reach.

Metropolitan Warehouse & Delivery Corp. is a trusted leader in premium furniture delivery and warehousing solutions, serving thousands of homes and businesses across the continental United States. With a focus on eCommerce logistics and white glove service, we support some of the most recognized brands in the industry.

We're actively seeking experienced, professional motor carriers who take pride in their work and share our commitment to excellence. If you own or operate a 26' box truck and specialize in residential or commercial furniture delivery, we invite you to partner with us.

Deliver with Metropolitan — and become part of a network that values reliability, professionalism, and long-term success.

Why Partner With Us

## Join a Premier Network of Furniture Delivery Experts.

Here's what sets a Metropolitan partnership apart.

#### Top-Tier Pay

We offer some of the most competitive rates in the industry — see for yourself.

#### Efficient Routes

Most routes complete in a single day, with options for one-, two-, or three-day runs.

#### Truck Leasing Made Easy

Take advantage of our lease-to-own straight truck opportunities, available directly through us.

#### Custom Mobile App

Our proprietary app streamlines operations and supports high-quality delivery performance.

Message From the CEO

## A Message From Our CEO & Founder, Shawn Khan.

Discover the vision behind Metropolitan Warehouse and Delivery as Shawn Khan shares his passion for excellence, the values that drive our company, and how we continue to raise the standard in white glove delivery.

From humble beginnings to a national presence, hear directly from the leader who built Metropolitan with a commitment to reliability, innovation, and long-term partnerships.

Shawn Khan

CEO & Founder, Metropolitan Warehouse & Delivery

Partner FAQs

## Your Guide to Partnering With Metropolitan.

Have questions about partnering with us? Below covers everything from getting started to understanding our support, tools, and expectations.

What are the requirements to partner with Metropolitan?

To qualify as a delivery partner with Metropolitan Warehouse and Delivery, all carriers must meet the following minimum requirements:

- 26' white box truck with liftgate and pallet jack
- Active Federal Motor Carrier Interstate Operating Authority
- Proven experience in final mile white glove home delivery, including setup, assembly, and installation
- Must be a registered LLC, Corporation, or Partnership (no sole proprietors); FEIN required
- Insurance coverage must meet the following minimums:
- - $1,000,000 Commercial Auto Liability
- $1,000,000 Commercial General Liability
- $100,000 Cargo Coverage
- Workers' Compensation: $500,000 or statutory minimums
- Criminal background and drug screening required for all delivery personnel
- Delivery teams must be capable of lifting, carrying, assembling, and installing furniture
- Availability required six days per week, including weekends
- All carrier personnel must speak English

What are your pay rates?

With over 44 hub locations across the United States, we offer some of the most competitive rates in the industry. To get detailed information on rates for your city and state, please reach out to our Recruitment Team.

Do you have specific routes?

Yes — we offer a wide range of routes conveniently located near our warehouse hubs. Whether you're looking for short, local deliveries or more extensive routes, we have options to suit your needs. For a personalized overview of the best routes available in your city and state, our Recruitment Team is ready to provide all the details and help you find the perfect fit.

What types of delivery services do you offer for your customers?

We offer a comprehensive range of delivery services designed to meet every need, including:

- Doorstep Delivery
- Threshold Delivery
- White Glove Service
- Premium White Glove Service
- Room of Choice Delivery
- Business-to-Business (B2B) Deliveries

Each service level is tailored to provide the highest quality experience for both residential and business customers. See our Services page for details or connect with our Recruitment Team.

Where do you have openings?

We are currently seeking carrier partners for several of our hub locations across the country. With over 44 facilities, there may be an opportunity near you. See the openings strip below for active recruiting locations.

# Shawn Khan, CEO & President of Metropolitan Warehouse & Delivery Corp, Real Leadership

From Real Leadership

### Episode Description

Shawn Khan’s entrepreneurial journey started from the ground up in a way most founders never experience. 

He didn’t inherit a company, raise venture capital, or even understand the industry he was stepping into.

Shawn bought a one-truck furniture delivery operation in New York City, rented the truck every morning, and learned the business by riding in the back making deliveries himself.

Two years later, he was ready to shut it down.

What changed everything wasn’t a new strategy. It was mentorship, perspective, and the willingness to stay in the fight long enough to evolve.

Today, Shawn leads Metropolitan Warehouse & Delivery, a company with 47 facilities nationwide, 3 million square feet of warehouse space, and partnerships with retailers like Costco, Amazon, Walmart, and Target.

But if you’re a leader, this episode isn’t just about logistics. It’s about: 

- How businesses actually scale.
- Surviving the early years when the numbers don’t work.
- Knowing when to expand and when expansion will hurt before it helps.
- Shifting from being the operator to building the system.
- Turning labor challenges into ownership opportunities.

Key Moments

01:37 – The search for a business

03:42 – The near-failure and the partner who changed everything

06:06 – Riding the e-commerce wave with Costco and Anthropology

07:56 – Doubling the business during the chaos of COVID-19

16:27 – Turning drivers into business owners through the contractor model

25:29 – Why logistics is now a technology business

Show Notes

### About this Podcast

#### Real Leadership

## Episode Transcript

00:00:00

The best thing that happened that helped our industry is e-commerce. You know, that's what just evolved everything. I mean, logistics business has completely changed. Welcome to Real Leadership, the show that cuts through the clutter to spotlight leaders who make, move and process things in the real economy.

00:00:24

This isn't about buzzwords or theories. It's about bold decisions, solving challenges and the strategies driving industries that matter. I'm Jim Weaver, CEO of The O'Neill Group. In every episode, we get real about what it takes to turn vision into action and obstacles into opportunities. Let's go.

00:00:45

Welcome back to Real Leadership. Today, our guest is Shawn Khan, founder, president, and CEO of Metropolitan Warehouse and Delivery, a logistics executive with more than 35 years of industry experience. Shawn founded Metropolitan Warehouse and Delivery in 1989 and has grown the company from a single location into a national provider of specialized furniture logistics and white glove delivery services.

00:01:12

Under his leadership, MWD supports furniture retailers, vendors, designers, and manufacturers with both B2B and direct-to-consumer operations, delivering full coverage across the lower 48. Today, the company operates in 47 U.S. facilities and over 3 million square feet of warehouse space, forming a nationwide infrastructure dedicated to furniture distribution and final mile delivery.

00:01:39

Shawn's entrepreneurial drive has positioned Metropolitan as a major force in shaping how furniture moves across America. Welcome, Shawn. Thank you. Thank you, Jim. How are we doing today? Doing great. Great. Thank you. Great to have you. Yeah. Okay, let's go back. Metropolitan Warehouse, big company today, huge footprint, but it didn't start out that way in 1989, did it? No.

00:02:03

Tell us how you got into the business, how this, the genesis of what is today Metropolitan Warehouse. Well, I was looking to be an entrepreneur and I was searching for like two to three years trying to find a business that I could buy. And there was really nothing that fit my budget. You know, it could have been anything.

00:02:26

It could have been a Dairy Queen, a Burger King, a 7-Eleven, a gas station, typical businesses that a lot of people start with. So I was just looking and I just stumbled across a guy who had a small warehouse and one truck operation delivering furniture for a furniture store in New York City. And I didn't even know what that business was. I had no idea that this type of business even existed.

00:02:54

So I met with him and he was sort of really looking to get out in a very quick way for whatever reason. And I struck a deal with him that I could afford. And I had another gentleman, one of my friends who became my partner and we bought the business from this gentleman. And the name of the company at that time was White Glove Warehouse. That was the name of the original company. So I got in.

00:03:21

It was a very small little account, one truck, which we would rent every day. We didn't even own a truck. We would rent it from budget and just go out and make deliveries. Were you actually delivering? Yes. Yes, I had to. I had to learn the business. You know, it took me a few years. Yeah, it would be two men. I had one employee and we would go out and make deliveries. I work in the office in the warehouse during the day. After lunch, go out and make deliveries and come back around dinner time. You're not making deliveries today, are you? No, no.

00:03:51

I stopped after about five years, yeah. You've been in it for 35 years. Companies usually sort of grow in spurts. So when did it click for you that, oh, this could be something bigger than I expected? Yeah, in the first two years was really, really difficult. And after two years of having my own company, which was called White Glove Warehouse, I was ready to bail. I was going to shut it down.

00:04:17

And one of my clients, really my only clients, I told them that I was shutting down. And the owner of that company came to me and said, why? And I said, I'm not making any money. It's a difficult business. I just don't have the financial capability to buy trucks and rent big buildings, which is needed. So he offered to become my investor. Oh, wow. But that's when we started, you know, Metropolitan Warehouse and Delivery in November of 1991.

00:04:47

But I always use 89 because that's when I started. And we just, you know, changed the name of the company because he joined as a partner. And we still work together from that day on. He's been my investor, my mentor. Everything that you can imagine that you need help with, he's been there for me.

00:05:21

So it's just a matter of needing to get over the hump from a capital standpoint. And when we started in 91, our idea was that we would, you know, grow the business to maybe five or 10 trucks and just be a very good company in the local New York metro market. And that's what we did for about almost 10 years.

00:05:45

And then after 10 years, we, you know, I learned a lot about the business and we opened our first location in North Carolina, High Point, which is sort of the furniture capital of the United States. Yes. And then I started to go to furniture shows and furniture markets. So, you know, we wanted to expand. There was a big connection between New York and North Carolina because the furniture is made there. So that was one part. So we started with a location in North Carolina.

00:06:11

And then our second location was in Miami, Florida in 2009. So we had three locations and we were pretty happy that we've expanded so much. And then around 2009 and 10, really when e-commerce furniture sales started to grow. And I guess I had a few customers. There were manufacturers of furniture that had some connections with some e-commerce companies, which they introduced me to them.

00:06:40

And that's where our business started to grow. You know, from 2010 through 2020, we went from three locations to like probably 40 locations. Wow. And it's all e-commerce. I met with big customers like Costco.com and Walmart and Target and even Amazon. We tried to do deliveries and a whole host of different e-commerce companies. So e-commerce is the main reason. Yeah. And then COVID hit. Yes.

00:07:10

And that was a pretty, yeah, significant for you, right? Yeah. In two years, we had so much. The first three months of COVID was very, very scary and obviously very difficult. But after that, you know, we were allowed to make deliveries as part of the, I guess they call them essential services. So we were allowed to go on the road. Our drivers had to wear masks and all that.

00:07:36

But e-commerce furniture sales just started to grow like this. And we had a really difficult time dealing with it because there was a really big shortage of labor. A lot of people didn't want to come to work. It was just a difficult time, but our business basically grew by 100% in exactly two years. Wow. Just 21 and 22. Our revenue grew by 100%.

00:08:01

And we went through a difficult time, but it was also a very good time because we kind of broke all the records. Yeah. So obviously the labor challenges during COVID is a huge factor. What were some of the other difficulties that you had to get past having that type of growth in just a couple of years, doubling your size?

00:08:25

We had to go out and try to secure more buildings because we didn't have enough space to handle the volume that we were getting. And during COVID, the industrial real estate market also just went through the roof. It was very, very hard. So in those two years, we planned and leased probably about 10 more cities we opened up. It took longer because during COVID, again, it was a lot of delays in construction and parts were not coming in.

# The final touch: Third-party providers focus on managing challenges, expectations

Furniture Today Staff// Staff Editors//June 30, 2025

##### By Powell Slaughter, Contributing Editor

ASHEVILLE, N.C. — Dealing with challenges, consumer expectations and evolving technology in final-mile service dominated a panel of third-party logistics providers at the recent AHFA/SFC Logistics Conference here.

Bluewater Logistics Group President and CEO Tiffany Bowman cited five headaches right now impacting getting goods into customers’ homes: high cost of operations, aging urban infrastructures that create congestion and cost time, the costs involved in reverse logistics when there’s a problem with damaged goods or incorrect orders and integrating client’s systems with the carrier’s.

Finding labor for drivers and handlers on the trucks and employees in the warehouse is Shawn Kahn’s biggest challenge right now.

See also: Gaining an inch with supply chain

“Nobody grows up wanting to become a delivery driver,” said Khan, president and CEO of Metropolitan Warehouse and Delivery.

Massood Logistics CEO Edward Massood and Cody Sides, director of transportation and finance for Deliveright Logistics, agreed with Khan that hiring, training and retaining the right people is their toughest problem these days.

“The first thing that makes it challenging to attract people is the sheer size and weight of the product; there’s a certain level of physical ability they need,” Massood said. “Then they have to navigate up stairs and through hallways that leads to damage.”

Sides noted that the delivery crew may well be the only human interaction a customer has with Deliveright’s e-commerce clients.

“They’re a direct representative of the e-commerce shipper,” he said, adding that another final-mile challenge is that most transportation management systems aren’t good at handling reverse logistics. “Nobody seems to want to handle that.”

#### Defining, managing expectations

What are the best ways to handle consumer expectations of white-glove and other sorts of final-mile service? Massood said a key is defining the elements of various delivery levels on the retail floor.

“What is white glove? What is threshold? Setting that expectation at the time of sale,” he said, offering examples of what to verify: Is the sales associate letting the customer know if a room has to be cleared? Does the delivery require a certificate of insurance? Does an elevator need to be reserved?

For its part, Metropolitan is spending a lot of money on training to clearly define for employees what white-glove service means. To that end, it established “Metropolitan University,” an ongoing program with constant training on service.

“Every morning we have a meeting to discuss what happened yesterday and ask what could happen today,” Khan said. “We go through scenarios, discuss which service is offered for a delivery.”

Sides said setting delivery expectations is one of Deliveright’s shipper customers’ most difficult tasks.

“They sell the dream, and we have to make the dream happen,” he said. “We have a team working with shippers to manage those expectations. We also explain what those different service levels mean, and include those communications in booking e-mails.”

#### Technology march

How are tracking and visibility technologies impacting final-mile logistics? Panelists were pleased generally with developments in such systems and software past years.

Deliveright uses Grasshopper, a proprietary tracking and routing technology it developed in-house, and Sides believes it’s a competitive advantage: “A lot of people are still in the situation we were in 20 years ago” for tracking.

Metropolitan also has an in-house system, Pinnacle, which Khan said was implemented in 2014 and “continues to improve.”

Massood was a retailer from 2001 to 2018 and watched the transitions in final-mile operations, service and technology go from “night to day,” crediting Dispatchtrack tracking and visibility software with changing the game.

He and other panelists said it’s extremely important to utilize photos of the delivery from start to finish.

“During the delivery process the team is taking photos from the empty room to the finished room,” he said. “That went to the designers to utilize as a re-sell or add-on sale with suggestions on what else might go in” the room.

“If there was damage, we knew the extent of the damage,” Massood added.

Bowman at Gulfstream noted those pictures should go with the order and “be available to anyone at any time.”

Photos also can helped better manage potential claims.

“Before, we had to send someone to the home to verify” any damage, Khan said. “The delivery team knows we use those pictures. We even have them take pictures of the hardware to make sure a bed can be set up.”

# Director, Operations

- METROPOLITAN WAREHOUSE AND DELIVERY - 3.1 
- Carneys Point, NJ

## Job Details

- Full-time
- $140,000 a year
- 1 day ago

## Benefits

- Paid holidays
- Health insurance
- Dental insurance
- 401(k)
- Paid time off
- Vision insurance
- Life insurance

## Qualifications

- Customer communication
- Managing teams as a warehouse supervisor

## Full Job Description

Director of Warehouse Operations

 About us:

 We are the growing leader in the furniture delivery industry. With multiple locations throughout the country, our goal is simple: To provide our clients and customers a 5 Star Delivery Experience.

 We are proud of our experienced, dedicated, and professional staff and as our rapid company growth continues we require that we constantly add motivated, enthusiastic individuals committed to providing the same exceptional customer service that is the hallmark of our success.

 Our mission is to ensure memories are delivered one piece of furniture at a time, on time, every time. We are looking for individuals experienced in logistics and transportation to add to our team who will contribute to achieving our mission.

 Job Summary:

 Metropolitan’s new Penns Grove / Carney’s Point, New Jersey Distribution Center is a major East Coast operation supporting multiple business segments, including 3PL warehousing, inbound receiving, fulfillment, cross-dock, linehaul, returns, and integration with Metropolitan’s final-mile delivery network.

 The Director of Operations is responsible for the overall performance of the facility, including safety, service, inventory accuracy, productivity, labor management, customer performance, financial results, building standards, and continuous improvement.

 As the leader of a new Metropolitan location, this position will play an important role in establishing the operating culture, developing the leadership team, implementing Metropolitan standards and systems, supporting customer onboarding, and scaling the operation as volume grows.

 The Director will work closely with Operations, Customer Success, Business Transformation, Quality, Safety, and other functional teams to ensure the facility delivers consistently against customer commitments and Metropolitan operating standards.

 Facility & Operational Leadership

- Provide overall leadership and accountability for warehouse operations within the Penns Grove / Carney’s Point Distribution Center.
- Strategically, manage the operation in accordance with Metropolitan policies, operating standards, customer requirements, and company objectives.
- Lead a 24/7 operating environment, including multiple shifts and seven-day-per-week operations as business requirements dictate.
- Establish and maintain a strong operating culture focused on safety, accountability, customer service, quality, productivity, and continuous improvement.
- Ensure appropriate management coverage and escalation processes across all shifts.
- Maintain effective communication and coordination between warehouse, transportation, linehaul, final-mile, customer service, and corporate functions.
- Ensure the facility is prepared to scale staffing, capacity, equipment, and processes as customer volume increases.

 New Facility Launch & Customer Onboarding

- Support the operational launch and stabilization of the new Penns Grove / Carney’s Point facility.
- Build and develop the facility leadership structure and operating routines.
- Partner with cross-functional teams on new customer implementations, inventory transitions, system setup, SOP development, testing, and go-live readiness.
- Ensure customer requirements are translated into clear operational processes and measurable performance standards.
- Support facility layout, workflow, storage utilization, MHE requirements, labor planning, and operational readiness.
- Lead post-launch stabilization and continuous improvement activities.

 Customer Service & SLA Performance

- Maintain strong customer relationships by ensuring timely response, issue resolution, and operational follow-through.
- Ensure execution against customer SLAs, contractual commitments, and Metropolitan service standards.
- Participate in customer business reviews and operational discussions as required.
- Identify service risks and operational exceptions early and implement corrective action before they negatively impact the customer.
- Partner with Customer Success and Account Management on root-cause analysis, corrective actions, and customer improvement plans.

 Inventory & Warehouse Execution

- Maintain high levels of inventory accuracy, location accuracy, barcode/scan compliance, receiving accuracy, picking accuracy, and shipping accuracy.
- Ensure disciplined execution of receiving, putaway, storage, picking, staging, loading, returns, and inventory control processes.
- Establish strong cycle-counting, inventory reconciliation, and root-cause processes.
- Ensure inventory discrepancies and operational exceptions are investigated and resolved promptly.
- Maintain warehouse organization, housekeeping, slotting, storage utilization, and dock discipline.
- Ensure proper handling and protection of furniture and other customer products throughout the facility.

 Labor & People Leadership

- Provide leadership and management oversight for all warehouse and applicable office personnel within the Distribution Center.
- Ensure staffing levels and schedules align with forecasted volume, customer requirements, productivity expectations, and financial targets.
- Optimize labor utilization while controlling overtime and temporary labor expense.
- Recruit, develop, coach, and retain a high-performing leadership and hourly workforce.
- Establish clear performance expectations and provide regular coaching and feedback.
- Ensure appropriate training and cross-training across operational functions.
- Maintain succession plans and leadership bench strength for critical roles.
- Partner with Human Resources to ensure employment practices comply with company policy and applicable federal, state, and local requirements.

 Productivity, Financial & Capacity Management

- Establish and maintain productivity standards
- Monitor labor productivity, cost per unit, cost per CFT, overtime, staffing, capacity utilization, and other operational cost drivers.
- Manage the facility within established operating budgets and financial expectations.
- Identify opportunities to improve labor efficiency, storage utilization, dock utilization, throughput, and overall operating cost.
- Ensure facility capacity is effectively managed across racked storage, bulk storage, staging, docks, and other operating areas.
- Support volume forecasting and capacity planning to ensure adequate labor, space, equipment, and resources.

 KPI & Performance Management

- Establish disciplined daily, weekly, and monthly operating reviews.
- Produce, analyze, and act upon operational data, reports, and performance trends.
- Maintain clear ownership of corrective actions when performance falls below target.
- Use data to identify root causes, operational trends, and improvement opportunities.
- Ensure management teams understand performance expectations and have visibility to results.

 Systems & Process Compliance

- Ensure consistent execution of Metropolitan Standard Operating Procedures throughout the facility.
- Participate in the implementation, testing, training, and adoption of new or upgraded warehouse, transportation, inventory, and reporting systems.
- Maintain a high level of WMS transaction and scan discipline.
- Ensure operational processes and system transactions accurately reflect the physical movement and status of inventory.
- Identify opportunities to automate processes, improve data quality, and increase operational visibility.

 Continuous Improvement

- Identify and execute Lean and continuous improvement opportunities that eliminate waste, reduce handling, improve flow, and increase productivity.
- Lead structured root-cause analysis and corrective action for recurring operational issues.
- Standardize successful processes across shifts and departments.
- Encourage employee participation in identifying safety, quality, service, and productivity improvements.

 Safety, Security & Facility Standards

- Maintain a strong safety culture and ensure compliance with applicable OSHA requirements and Metropolitan safety policies.
- Identify and drive safety improvements throughout the Distribution Center.
- Ensure appropriate training and safe operation of forklifts, turret trucks, pallet jacks, dock

 equipment, and other material handling equipment.

- Maintain standards for facility cleanliness, housekeeping, hygiene, security, emergency preparedness, and access control.
- Ensure aisles, docks, exits, egress paths, storage areas, and work areas remain safe and compliant.
- Coordinate building maintenance and facility-related issues with the appropriate internal and external partners.
- Ensure incidents, injuries, product damage, and safety concerns are investigated and corrective actions are implemented.

 Key Performance Indicators

 Performance will be measured across key operational areas, including:

- Customer SLA attainment
- On-time receiving and dock-to-stock performance
- Order processing and fulfillment performance
- Inventory accuracy
- Receiving, picking, shipping, and scan accuracy
- Product damage and warehouse claims
- Labor productivity and utilization
- Overtime and temporary labor management
- Operating cost performance
- Storage and facility capacity utilization
- Dock and throughput performance
- Safety incidents and corrective action closure
- Employee turnover, attendance, and training completion
- Customer escalations and issue resolution
- SOP and process compliance
- Continuous improvement and cost-saving initiatives
- Facility financial performance versus budget

 Qualifications

- Bachelor’s degree in Supply Chain, Logistics, Operations Management, Business, or related field preferred.
- Minimum 10 years of progressive operations experience in a high-volume warehouse, distribution, fulfillment, or logistics environment preferred.
- Minimum 5 years of leadership experience, including responsibility for managers, supervisors, and hourly employees.
- Experience managing a large, multi-shift distribution operation strongly preferred.
- Experience with 3PL warehousing, furniture, big-and-bulky products, home furnishings, or final-mile logistics preferred.
- Experience opening, expanding, relocating, or stabilizing a distribution center is highly desirable.
- Demonstrated ability to manage customer SLAs, KPIs, productivity standards, budgets, and financial targets.
- Strong understanding of warehouse management systems and inventory control processes.
- Strong knowledge of receiving, putaway, storage, picking, shipping, cross-dock, returns, and inventory management.
- Working knowledge of OSHA requirements and warehouse safety practices.
- Working knowledge of warehouse material handling equipment and MHE safety requirements.
- Working knowledge of applicable federal, state, and local employment requirements.
- Strong analytical and problem-solving skills with the ability to use operational data to identify root causes and drive action.
- High proficiency with Microsoft Office, particularly Excel.
- Experience implementing organizational and process change within a distribution environment.
- Strong leadership, communication, coaching, and employee-development skills.
- Ability to manage multiple priorities in a fast-paced, high-growth environment.
- Ability and availability to work irregular or extended hours, including nights, weekends, and holidays, as operational needs require.

 Leadership Profile

 The successful candidate will be a visible, hands-on operations leader who can move comfortably between the warehouse floor, customer discussions, performance data, and strategic planning. This individual must be able to establish accountability, develop people, solve problems quickly, and build scalable processes while maintaining a strong focus on safety and the customer experience.

 Because this is a new and strategically important Metropolitan facility, the Director will be expected not only to run warehouse operation, but also to build and continuously improve it as the business grows.

- Medical/Dental/Vision Insurance
- 401(K) Plan
- Life Insurance
- Paid Holidays
- Paid Time Off (PTO)

 Metropolitan Warehouse is an equal opportunity employer. All applicants will be considered for employment without attention to race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, veteran, or disability status.
